Enriched string-net models and their excitations
David Green, Peter Huston, Kyle Kawagoe, David Penneys, Anup Poudel, Sean Sanford

Abstract
Boundaries of Walker-Wang models have been used to construct commuting projector models which realize chiral unitary modular tensor categories (UMTCs) as boundary excitations. Given a UMTC 𝒜 \mathcal{A} representing the Witt class of an anomaly, the article [arXiv:2208.14018] gave a commuting projector model associated to an 𝒜 \mathcal{A} -enriched unitary fusion category 𝒳 {\mathcal{X}} on a 2D boundary of the 3D Walker-Wang model associated to 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . That article claimed that the boundary excitations were given by the enriched center/Müger centralizer Z 𝒜 ​ ( 𝒳 ) Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}) of 𝒜 {\mathcal{A}} in Z ⁡ ( 𝒳 ) Z({\mathcal{X}}) . In this article, we give a rigorous treatment of this 2D boundary model, and we verify this assertion using topological quantum field theory (TQFT) techniques, including skein modules and a certain semisimple algebra whose representation category describes boundary excitations. We also use TQFT techniques to show the 3D bulk point excitations of the Walker-Wang bulk are given by the Müger center Z 2 ​ ( 𝒜 ) Z_{2}(\mathcal{A}) , and we construct bulk-to-boundary hopping operators Z 2 ​ ( 𝒜 ) → Z 𝒜 ​ ( 𝒳 ) Z_{2}(\mathcal{A})\to Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}) reflecting how the UMTC of boundary excitations Z 𝒜 ​ ( 𝒳 ) Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}) is symmetric-braided enriched in Z 2 ​ ( 𝒜 ) Z_{2}(\mathcal{A}) . This article also includes a self-contained comprehensive review of the Levin-Wen string net model from a unitary tensor category viewpoint, as opposed to the skeletal 6j symbol viewpoint.



1]The Ohio State University
2]Vanderbilt University

1
Introduction

One of the most powerful features of topologically ordered phases of matter
[
Wen17
]
is the robustness of their relevant properties under perturbation
[
Wen90
,
WN90
]
.
As an example, despite the fact that Laughlin’s wavefunction
[
Lau83
]
is not a precise solution to the problem of an electron gas in the presence of a magnetic field, it accurately captures the phenomena of fractionalized charge and fractionally quantized Hall conductance.
Furthering this philosophy, Levin and Wen wrote down their famous string-net models
[
LW05
]
, which made concrete the connection between fusion categories and the physics they represent.

String net models condense topological order from the vacuum; indeed, a fusion category
{\mathcal{X}}
is a condensable algebra in the symmetric monoidal 2-category
2\mathsf{Vect}

[
GJF19
,
JFR24
]
.
The procedure to condense
{\mathcal{X}}

[
Mul22
]
corresponds to passing to the ground state space of the commuting projector Levin-Wen local Hamiltonian
[
LW05
,
LLB21
]
, whose localized excitations can be described by the Drinfeld center
Z({\mathcal{X}})

[
KKR10
,
Kir11
]
, which is Witt-equivalent to the trivial topological order
\mathsf{Vect}

[
DMNO13
]
.

It is widely accepted that (2+1)D commuting projector models produce exactly those unitary modular tensor categories (UMTCs) which are Drinfeld centers as their categories of localized anyonic excitations.
In particular, chiral UMTCs should only appear as boundaries of invertible (3+1)D topological quantum field theories (TQFTs)
[
JF22
,
FT21
]
, which correspond to the anomaly
[
KT17
]
.
This anomaly can be represented by a Witt-class
[
DMNO13
]
of UMTCs
[
BJSS21
]
.
This is a manifestation of a bulk-boundary correspondence; such correspondences appear throughout topological physics
[
Wen95
,
Wen13
,
Lev13
,
KWZ17
]
.

To build a (3+1)D commuting projector model which realizes a chiral UMTC
{\mathcal{C}}
as boundary excitations, we first fix a UMTC
{\mathcal{A}}
representing the anomaly.
We then choose an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched unitary fusion category
({\mathcal{X}},\Phi^{Z})
, i.e. a unitary fusion category (UFC)
{\mathcal{X}}
equipped with a unitary braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})

[
HBJP23
, § II.B]
, so that the centralizer
Z^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}})
of
\Phi^{Z}({\mathcal{A}})
in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
is
{\mathcal{C}}
.
The functor
\Phi^{Z}
is the data necessary to attach a (2+1)D Levin-Wen model
[
LW05
]
for
{\mathcal{X}}
as the boundary of a
(3+1)D Walker-Wang model
[
WW12
]
for
{\mathcal{A}}
(in red below).
We write
\Phi:=F\circ\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{X}}
, where
F:Z({\mathcal{X}})\to{\mathcal{X}}
is the forgetful functor.

a
x_{1}
x_{2}
y_{1}
y_{2}
{\mathcal{X}}(\Phi({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}a})y_{1}x_{1}\to x_{2}y_{2})
a_{2}
a_{1}
c_{1}
c_{2}
b_{2}
b_{1}
{\mathcal{A}}(a_{1}b_{1}c_{1}\to c_{2}b_{2}a_{2})

The local Hamiltonian is made up of 1D edge terms and 2D plaquette terms for every 2D square in the lattice. The half-braiding for
\Phi(a)
with
{\mathcal{X}}
is used in a crucial way to define the plaquette terms at the interface of the 3D bulk with the 2D boundary.
We refer the reader to §
3
below for more details.
We remark that related (2+1)D boundary theories for (3+1)D Walker-Wang models also appear in
[
BCFV14
,
vKBS13
]
.

These
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched string net models condense topological order Witt equivalent to
{\mathcal{A}}
from
{\mathcal{A}}
-topological order;
indeed an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched fusion category is a condensable algebra in the fusion 2-category
\mathsf{Mod}({\mathcal{A}})

[
Déc23
, Ex. 1.4.6]
.
Condensing
{\mathcal{X}}
(cf.
[
Mul22
]
) corresponds to passing to the ground state space of our
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched string net local Hamiltonian, whose localized excitations can be described by the enriched center
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}):={\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}\subset Z({\mathcal{X}})

[
KZ18
]
,
which is Witt-equivalent to
{\mathcal{A}}

[
DMNO13
]
.

It was claimed in
[
HBJP23
, § II.B]
that the topological excitations which live on the boundary of the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched string net model for
{\mathcal{X}}
are described by the enriched center
Z^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}})
, i.e., the Müger centralizer of
{\mathcal{A}}
in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
We give a rigorous proof of this fact using
TQFT techniques, including
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched skein modules for
{\mathcal{X}}
and the
dome algebra

\operatorname{Dome}^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}})
, a certain quotient of the tube algebra
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})

[
Izu01
,
Müg03
]
.
In an ordinary (2+1)D string-net model, the algebra
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
acts as local operators near the site of a topological excitation, so that anyon types correspond to (isomorphism classes of) indecomposable representations of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
.
The presence of the (3+1)D
{\mathcal{A}}
-bulk induces additional requirements on topological local operators, which cuts down
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
to
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}})
.

The structure of this paper is as follows.
First, §
2
is a self-contained primer on the Levin-Wen string net model
[
LW05
]
from a unitary tensor category viewpoint.
For simplicity, we use a square lattice, and all degrees of freedom occur at vertices, similar to
[
Kon14
]
.
In §
2.1
, we define the disk skein module associated to a UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
, and prove basic results about skein modules which will be used throughout the paper.
In §
2.2
, we provide some helpful conceptual proofs of well-known facts in the literature, including the matrix coefficients for the plaquette operators in Lemma
2.8
and the proof that the product of all plaquette operators is a scalar multiple of the projection to the skein module in Theorem
2.9
.
We also give an elegant description of the ground state space of the edge terms in terms of hom spaces in the UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
in Proposition
2.6
.
In §
2.3
, we review the basics of the tube algebra
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
and give the well-known correspondence between its category of representations and objects in
Z({\mathcal{X}})

[
Izu01
]
.
In §
2.4
, we fully describe excitations localized on one edge and its two adjacent plaquettes, together with a shortened and simplified presentation of general string operators and their connection to
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
-representations from
[
CGHP23
]
.
Finally, in §
2.5
, we give a shortened and simplified presentation of hopping operators from
[
CGHP23
]
.

Next, we analyze the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched string net model for an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC introduced in
[
HBJP23
, II.B]
in §
3
.
We do so in more generality, assuming that
{\mathcal{A}}
is unitary braided (but not necessarily modular), but still requiring
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
to be fully faithful.
In §
3.1
, we give explicit detail on the plaquette operators and their connection to
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched skein modules.
In §
3.2
, we introduce the
dome algebra

\operatorname{Dome}^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
, communicated to us by Corey Jones and inspired by Kevin Walker, which is a quotient of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
by an ideal
{\mathcal{J}}^{\mathcal{A}}
coming from the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enrichment.
The point of
\operatorname{Dome}^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
is Theorem
3.9
which shows that
\mathsf{Rep}(\operatorname{Dome}^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}))\cong Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
, the enriched center
[
KZ18
]
of
{\mathcal{X}}
.
We then show that our
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
-action on the
{\mathcal{X}}
string net model also gives an action on our
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched model which descends to an action of
\operatorname{Dome}^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
.
Our ideal
{\mathcal{J}}^{\mathcal{A}}
acts as zero on
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
-representations from precisely those string operators corresponding to anyons in
\operatorname{Irr}(Z^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}}))
, so localized enriched excitations exactly correspond to the enriched center
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
as claimed in
[
HBJP23
]
.
Finally, in §
3.4
, we analyze bulk excitations using the
sphere algebra
of
{\mathcal{A}}
, again communicated to us by Corey Jones and inspired by Kevin Walker.
Our analysis is consistent with
[
JFR24
, Lem. 2.16]
; the point excitations in the bulk are
\Omega Z(\Sigma{\mathcal{A}})=Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
.
Under the additional assumption that the braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
is full,
Z_{2}(Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}))=Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
by
[
DNO13
, Prop. 4.3]
, and the canonical map is exactly bringing a bulk excitation to the boundary via a modified hopping operator.

2
String net models for unitary fusion categories

Here we review the commuting projector Levin-Wen string net model built from a unitary fusion category (UFC)
{\mathcal{X}}
, including the braided category of excitations and string operators.
General references include

[
EGNO15
]
for fusion categories,

[
HP17
,
Pen20
]
for UFCs, and

[
LW05
,
Kon14
,
LLB21
]
for 2D Levin-Wen string net models.
In particular, we always equip our UFC with its canonical unitary spherical structure, allowing us to form closed diagrams on a sphere which are invariant under isotopy.

We view these 2D string net models as condensing topological order from the vacuum, which is mathematically supported by
[
GJF19
,
Mul22
,
JF22
]
and informs our diagrammatic calculus of shaded regions.
Starting from the vacuum, from any UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
one can attach a finite dimensional Hilbert space built from hom spaces in
{\mathcal{X}}
to every vertex of a square lattice as in the first picture below.
Enforcing the consistency condition that labels of simple objects on edges/links (the
A_{\ell}
terms) has the effect of condensing a 1-skeleton.
Passing to the image of the plaquette/face operators (the
B_{p}
terms) allows isotopy across each plaquette, effectively condensing 2-cells onto the 1-skeleton.

{\mathcal{X}}
is a unitary fusion category and
\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
is the set of isomorphism classes of simple objects of
{\mathcal{X}}

Indeed, there is a non-zero map
1_{\mathcal{X}}\to z
if and only if
z=1_{\mathcal{X}}
.
In this case,

\overline{y}=x
and
\{\operatorname{ev}_{x}\}
is an ONB of
{\mathcal{X}}(\overline{x}x\to 1_{\mathcal{X}})\subset{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},3)
.

We define a gluing map
\operatorname{gl}:{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+1)\otimes{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},n+1)\to{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+n)

Lemma 2.4
.

The gluing map (
1
) restricts to a unitary on the subspace of
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+1)\otimes{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},n+1)
where
x_{m+1}=\overline{y_{1}}
.
In particular, gluing two ONBs for
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+1)
and
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},n+1)

whose string labels match appropriately
gives an ONB for
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+n)
.

Proof.

When the appropriate labels of
f,g
match (
x_{m+1}=\overline{y_{1}}
)
as well as those of
f^{\prime},g^{\prime}
(
x_{m+1}^{\prime}=\overline{y_{1}^{\prime}}
),
applying Fact
2.3
in the sideways direction yields

\displaystyle\langle\operatorname{gl}(f\otimes g)|\operatorname{gl}(f^{\prime}\otimes g^{\prime})\rangle

\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\delta_{x_{i}=x_{i}^{\prime}}}{\sqrt{d_{x_{i}}}}\prod_{j=2}^{n+1}\frac{\delta_{y_{j}=y_{j}^{\prime}}}{\sqrt{d_{y_{j}}}}\right)\cdot\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to128.12pt{\vbox to75.18pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 35.22041pt\lower-9.1359pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

\displaystyle=\langle f|f^{\prime}\rangle\cdot\langle g|g^{\prime}\rangle=\langle f\otimes g|g\otimes g^{\prime}\rangle.\qed

We end with the following observation about
how morphism spaces act on skein modules.
First, using the unitary spherical structure of
{\mathcal{X}}
, we may identify

{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+n)\cong\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\\
y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\\
\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})\end{subarray}}{\mathcal{X}}(x_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{m}\to y_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes y_{n}).

Given a map
f:y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\to z_{1},\dots,z_{p}
,
we may consider the map
\gamma_{f}
that post-composes with
f
when the string labels agree and gives zero otherwise.
One computes that for
g\in{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+n)
and
h\in{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},m+p)

\displaystyle\langle h|\gamma_{f}g\rangle

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{x_{1}}\cdots d_{x_{m}}d_{z_{1}}\cdots d_{z_{p}}}}\cdot\operatorname{tr}_{\mathcal{X}}(h^{\dagger}\circ f\circ g)

\displaystyle\langle\gamma_{f^{\dagger}}h|g\rangle

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{x_{1}}\cdots d_{x_{m}}d_{y_{1}}\cdots d_{y_{n}}}}\cdot\operatorname{tr}_{\mathcal{X}}((f^{\dagger}\circ h)^{\dagger}\circ g).

Thus we see that

\gamma_{f}^{\dagger}=\frac{\sqrt{d_{y_{1}}\cdots d_{y_{n}}}}{\sqrt{d_{z_{1}}\cdots d_{z_{p}}}}\gamma_{f^{\dagger}}.

Definition 2.5
.

We define
\Gamma_{f}
to be the operator which post-composes with
f
and multiplies by a scalar factor as in
[
CGHP23
]
so that
\Gamma_{f}^{\dagger}=\Gamma_{f^{\dagger}}
on the nose:

(2)

\Gamma_{f}:=\left(\frac{d_{z_{1}}\cdots d_{z_{p}}}{d_{y_{1}}\cdots d_{y_{n}}}\right)^{1/4}\cdot\gamma_{f}.

is a unitary fusion category.

{\mathcal{X}}
and the lattice.

The total Hilbert space is
{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}:=\bigotimes_{v}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
, represented by the disconnected lattice above, in which the gray region is vacuum.
The lattice is directed by the blue arrows in the above figure, so that every edge has an incoming and outgoing vertex.
The next step is to define the low-energy Hilbert space.
We do this by defining the two terms that make up the Hamiltonian
H
.

First,
for each edge
\ell
, the term
A_{\ell}
is a projector onto states where the types of simple objects labeling the two halves of
\ell
match.
Let
P_{A}
denote the projection onto the ground state space of
-\sum_{\ell}A_{\ell}
.
Passing to
P_{A}{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
has the effect of connecting the edges to condense the 1-skeleton of the lattice above.

There is an elegant description of
P_{A}{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
in terms of the UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
.
Let
I:{\mathcal{X}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
be the adjoint of the forgetful functor
F:Z({\mathcal{X}})\to{\mathcal{X}}

[
Müg03
, Prop. 8.1]
, for which there are canonical natural isomorphisms

{\mathcal{X}}(F(X)\to y)\cong Z({\mathcal{X}})(X\to I(y))\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\forall\,X\in Z({\mathcal{X}})\quad\forall\,y\in{\mathcal{X}}.

In particular, we have the formula
FI(x)=\bigoplus_{y\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})}yx\overline{y}
.

Proposition 2.6
.

On a contractible patch
\Lambda
of lattice that contains
\#p=\#p(\Lambda)
many plaquettes,

P_{A}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}=\bigoplus_{\vec{x}\in\partial\Lambda}{\mathcal{X}}(\vec{x}\to FI(1_{\mathcal{X}})^{\otimes\#p}),

where
\vec{x}
denotes a boundary condition, i.e., a tensor product over the simple labels
x_{i}
on the boundary of
\Lambda
, and we sum over the set
\partial\Lambda
of all such boundary conditions.

Proof.

We begin with the analysis of a single plaquette, which should be viewed as having a puncture in it corresponding to the vacuum.
Using Fact
2.3
three times, we glue the 4 copies of
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},4)
along matched boundary conditions to obtain

\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}g,h,i,j\\
s,\cdots,z\\

As this diagram is a closed diagram in
{\mathcal{X}}
, we can apply the (
Fusion
) relation again to ‘unzip’ along the
r
string to obtain (
4
) as claimed.

To see that
B_{p}
is self-adjoint, we simply observe
C(\eta,\xi)=\overline{C(\xi,\eta)}
, and thus the matrix representation of
B_{p}
is self-adjoint.
That
B_{p}^{2}=B_{p}
and
[B_{p},B_{q}]=0
for distinct plaquettes
p,q
follows from (
I=H
) and (
Bigon 2
) as depicted in
[
Zha17
, §5.4]
.
∎

The string-net local Hamiltonian is given by

(5)

H:=-\sum_{\ell}A_{\ell}-\sum_{p}B_{p}.

We can describe the ground state space of
H
in terms of skein modules for
{\mathcal{X}}

[
Kon14
]
.
There is an obvious
evaluation map

\operatorname{eval}:P_{A}{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}\to{\mathcal{S}}({\mathbb{D}},N)
given by evaluating a morphism in the skein module, where
N
is the number of external edges of our lattice.
The following result is claimed in
[
Kon14
]
; we give a short conceptual proof for convenience and completeness.
We will prove an enriched version in §
3
below.

Theorem 2.9

(
[
Kon14
]
)
.

On
P_{A}{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
,
\prod_{p}B_{p}=D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-\#p}\operatorname{eval}^{\dagger}\circ\operatorname{eval}
,
where
\#p
is the number of plaquettes in the lattice.

Proof.

The proof proceeds by adjoining adjacent plaquettes by induction.
We provide the detailed argument for 2 adjacent plaquettes
o,p
, and we leave the remaining details to the reader.
We will show that if
\xi,\xi^{\prime}
are choices of 6 vectors from our distinguished ONB of
{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
,

\langle\xi|B_{o}B_{p}\xi^{\prime}\rangle_{\bigotimes_{v\in{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}}=D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-2}\langle\operatorname{eval}\xi|\operatorname{eval}\xi^{\prime}\rangle_{{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},10)}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad B_{o}B_{p}=D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-2}\operatorname{eval}^{\dagger}\circ\operatorname{eval}.

To ease the notation, we set

\displaystyle K

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{q}d_{r}d_{s}d_{t}d_{u}d_{v}d_{w}d_{x}d_{y}d_{z}}},

\displaystyle K_{o}

\displaystyle:=\frac{\sqrt{d_{j}d_{h}d_{m}d_{g}}}{\sqrt{d_{j^{\prime}}d_{h^{\prime\prime}}d_{m^{\prime}}d_{g^{\prime}}}}

\displaystyle K_{o}^{\prime}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{j}d_{j^{\prime}}d_{h}d_{m}d_{m^{\prime}}d_{g}d_{g^{\prime}}}},

\displaystyle K_{p}(h^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle:=\frac{\sqrt{d_{k}d_{i}d_{\ell}d_{h^{\prime\prime}}}}{\sqrt{d_{k^{\prime}}d_{i^{\prime}}d_{\ell^{\prime}}d_{h^{\prime}}}}

\displaystyle K_{p}^{\prime}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}d_{k^{\prime}}d_{i}d_{i^{\prime}}d_{\ell}d_{\ell^{\prime}}d_{h^{\prime}}}}.

In the calculation below, we label strings and vertices as much as possible, but sometimes we omit labels that can be determined from the previous diagram when the diagram is getting very intricate.
Moreover, since we have fixed
\eta_{i,j}\in\operatorname{ONB}
, some of the sums over simples from the plaquette operators collapse as in the proof of Lemma
2.8
.
We suppress shadings on squares for readability.

Remark 2.10
.

Under the unitary isomorphism from Proposition
2.6
, the operator
B_{p}
corresponds to a
Kirby element
of
{\mathcal{X}}
(see
[
Vir06
, Def. 2.1]
) using the strings on tubes graphical calculus from
[
HPT16
,
HPT23a
]
.
Here, we require that
I:{\mathcal{X}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
is the right unitary adjoint of
F:Z({\mathcal{X}})\to{\mathcal{X}}
from
[
HPT23b
, §2.1]
.
Recall that
\operatorname{End}_{Z({\mathcal{X}})}(I(1_{\mathcal{X}}))\cong K_{0}({\mathcal{X}})
, the fusion algebra of
{\mathcal{X}}
, as

\operatorname{End}_{Z({\mathcal{X}})}(I(1_{\mathcal{X}}))\cong{\mathcal{X}}(FI(1_{\mathcal{X}})\to 1_{\mathcal{X}})\cong\bigoplus_{x\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})}{\mathcal{X}}(\overline{x}x\to 1_{\mathcal{X}}).

We write
i:1_{\mathcal{X}}\to I(1_{\mathcal{X}})=IF(1_{Z({\mathcal{X}})})
for the unit of the adjunction, and we have
i^{\dagger}\circ i=1_{\mathbb{C}}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{X}}(1_{\mathcal{X}})
by
[
HPT23b
, Lem. 3.8]
.

[
EGNO15
, Prop. 3.3.6]
, we see that

2.3
The tube algebra

Suppose
{\mathcal{X}}
is a unitary fusion category.
We review Ocneanu’s
tube algebra
, which is a powerful tool for calculating the Drinfeld center
Z({\mathcal{X}})

[
Izu01
,
Müg03
]
.
Let
\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
denote a set of representatives of the simple objects of
{\mathcal{X}}
.
We suppress tensor symbols, associators, and unitors whenever possible.

Definition 2.11
.

The
tube algebra
of
{\mathcal{X}}
is the finite dimensional
\rm C^{*}
-algebra

\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}}):=\bigoplus_{v,x,y\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})}{\mathcal{X}}(vx\to yv)

with multiplication and adjoint given respectively by

\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to42.54pt{\vbox to41.26pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 20.12997pt\lower-21.13771pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{{}}{}
{}{}{}{}{{}}{}{}{}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{}{}{{}}}{{}{}{{}}}{}{}{{}{}{{}}}{{}{}{{}}}{}{}{{}{}{{}}}{{}{}{{}}}{}{}{{}{}{{}}}{{}{}{{}}}{}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -19.69 -11.81 M -19.69 -4.89 L -19.69 4.89 C -19.69 8.71 -16.59 11.81 -12.77 11.81 L 12.77 11.81 C 16.59 11.81 19.69 8.71 19.69 4.89 L 19.69 -4.89 C 19.69 -8.71 16.59 -11.81 12.77 -11.81 L -12.77 -11.81 C -16.59 -11.81 -19.69 -8.71 -19.69 -4.89 Z M 19.69 11.81}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{}{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}{}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{}{}{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}{}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{{}}{}{{}}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

There is a well-known equivalence of categories
\mathsf{Rep}(\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}}))\simeq Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
Our convention for
Z({\mathcal{X}})
is that objects
(X,\sigma_{X})\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
will be denoted by pairs consisting of an upper-case Roman letter and a lower-case Greek letter, usually
\sigma
or
\tau
representing the half-braiding. Our graphical calculus for
\sigma_{X}
is that the string for
X
, which is drawn in color, goes
under
to signify that
\sigma_{X}
is natural with respect to all morphisms in
{\mathcal{X}}
, but only special morphisms in
{\mathcal{X}}
define morphisms in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
.

indexed by ONBs

\displaystyle\left\{(f,m)\middle|f\in{\mathcal{X}}(vy\to x),\,m\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to y)\right\}

and

\displaystyle\left\{(g,n)\middle|g\in{\mathcal{X}}(zv\to x),\,n\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to z)\right\}

for

\displaystyle{\mathcal{X}}(vX\to x)\cong\bigoplus_{y\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})}{\mathcal{X}}(vy\to x)\otimes{\mathcal{X}}(X\to y)

and

\displaystyle{\mathcal{X}}(Xv\to x)\cong\bigoplus_{z\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})}{\mathcal{X}}(zv\to x)\otimes{\mathcal{X}}(X\to z).

Conversely, these matrix elements completely determine
\sigma_{X,v}
.
Thus, given a
*
-representation
{\mathcal{H}}
of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
,
we use the minimal central idempotents
p_{x}\in\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
for
x\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
to get an object in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
by

X_{\mathcal{H}}:=\bigoplus_{y\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})}p_{y}{\mathcal{H}}\rhd y

using the canonical
\mathsf{Hilb}
-module structure of
{\mathcal{X}}
.
Observe that we have a canonical identification
{\mathcal{X}}(X_{{\mathcal{H}}}\to y)=p_{y}{\mathcal{H}}
by the Yoneda Lemma.
The half-braiding
\sigma_{{\mathcal{H}}_{X}}
is defined by the matrix-unit formula above.

2.4
Localized excitations, punctured skein modules, and string operators

Violations of the terms in the Hamiltonian (
5
)
restricted to a small region of the lattice represent localized excitations.
In this section,
we consider only the excitations that are localized on one edge and its two adjacent plaquettes.
Such excitations violate (at most) 3 terms in the Hamiltonian, and can be viewed as elements in a punctured skein module
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{A}},n,2)
(where
{\mathbb{A}}
denotes the annulus) with
n
external boundary points and 2 internal boundary points.

excitation
\scriptstyle v
\scriptstyle\ell

Now applying the fusion relation to both
\operatorname{id}_{z\overline{w}}
and
\operatorname{id}_{y\overline{x}}
exhibits
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
as a full corner.

By the above discussion, without loss of generality, we may focus our attention on the subspace of
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{A}},n,1)\subset{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{A}},n,2)
where the top section of the broken edge is labelled by
\textbf{1}_{X}
.
That is, we project to the image of the operator
\pi^{1}_{\ell,v}
which enforces that the edge label on
\ell
adjacent to the vertex
v
is
1_{\mathcal{X}}
:

excitation
\scriptstyle v
\scriptstyle\ell

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{1}_{\ell,v}}

We now describe the action of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
on
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{A}},n,1)
and construct a unitary isomorphism (as a tube algebra representation) to a direct sum of regular representations of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
.
Suppose we have a state
|\Omega\rangle
which is in the ground state of every
-A_{k}
for
k\neq\ell
and every
-B_{p}
except the two plaquettes adjacent to
\ell
.
We further assume that
|\Omega\rangle=\pi^{1}_{\ell,v}|\Omega\rangle
.
The action of
f\in{\mathcal{X}}(sy\to zs)\subset\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
on
|\Omega\rangle
is given similar to a plaquette operator:

where suppress the sum over simples and the resulting scalars in the final diagram.
We can thus classify all localized excitations as irreducible representations of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
, which correspond to the anyon types in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
The scalar
(d_{z}/d_{x})^{1/4}
is needed (see (
2
) above) to make this representation of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
a
*
-representation.

To see that all such anyons arise as excitations, we now define our
string operators
as operators from the space of ground states to a twice punctured skein module living inside
{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
.
Given
(X,\sigma_{X})\in\operatorname{Irr}(Z({\mathcal{X}}))
,
x,y\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
,
\psi\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to x)
,
\phi\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to y)
, two distinct edges
k,\ell
of our lattice (which we assume are separated by several plaquettes), and a path
\gamma:\ell\to k
on our lattice,
we get the string operator
S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\gamma}(\phi,\psi)

on a ground state
|\Omega\rangle

by first applying
\pi_{\ell}^{1}\pi_{k}^{1}
and then ‘inserting’ the
(X,\sigma_{X})
string, where
\phi
and
\psi
are used at the endpoints of the string to obtain an element in
{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
.
Here, for an edge
\ell
,
\pi_{\ell}^{1}
is the projection on
{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
which enforces both edge labels on
\ell
to be
1_{\mathcal{X}}
.
We include a cartoon below of one side of the string operator:

\scriptstyle\ell
\scriptstyle p
\scriptstyle q

\scriptstyle p\vee q

\scriptstyle X
\scriptstyle\psi

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\ell}^{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\gamma}(\bullet,\psi)}

Remark 2.12
.

Recall that our convention for half-braidings in (
6
) is that we always write the object in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
as passing
below
objects in
{\mathcal{X}}
.
Here, we have instead drawn our excitations as living
above
the
{\mathcal{X}}
-lattice.
That is, we are using the convention

This convention will be useful in the enriched setting in §
3
below.
There, we use an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
to construct a (2+1)D boundary for the (3+1)D
{\mathcal{A}}
-Walker-Wang model.
We show in Theorem
3.9
below that the boundary excitations are given by the enriched center
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}):={\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}\subset Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
We draw these excitations on the opposite side of the enriching lattice for clarity, viewing
{\mathcal{X}}
as an
{\mathcal{A}}-Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})^{\operatorname{rev}}
bimodule tensor category as
Z({\mathcal{X}})\cong{\mathcal{A}}\boxtimes Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
.

As with plaquette operators, we must resolve this final picture into
{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
;
to do so, we decompose
F(X,\sigma_{X})=X\in{\mathcal{X}}
into simples, where
F:Z({\mathcal{X}})\to{\mathcal{X}}
is the forgetful functor, and use (
Fusion
).
We include a cartoon below, where we suppress sums over simples and ONBs and scalars to ease the notation.

again suppressing sums over simples and the resulting scalars
K
in the final diagram.
This means
\pi^{1}_{\ell}|\Omega\rangle
is a ground state on the mutated lattice with a modified local Hamiltonian.
This means that on the space of ground states,

S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\gamma}(\phi,\psi)=S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\gamma}(\phi,\psi)\pi^{1}_{\ell}=S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\gamma}(\phi,\psi)B_{p\vee q}\pi^{1}_{\ell},

so one can encircle the end of the string operator by a
B_{p\vee q}
:

This is an amplification of Izumi’s action of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
corresponding to
(X,\sigma_{X})
; the scalar in front appears only because we use a different inner product for the punctured skein module than Izumi uses.
We therefore see that all simple objects in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
arise as localized excitations, and every excitation corresponds to some simple object in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
.

Remark 2.13
.

Local operators cannot change the anyon type of a localized excitation.
Consider a twice-punctured sphere where the punctures are sufficiently separated.
We claim the space of ground-states on this punctured sphere is exactly
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
, which carries commuting left and right actions of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
, one action at each puncture.
Indeed, by a variant of Proposition
2.6
, the ground state space of our twice punctured sphere with boundary strands that can host excitations is given by

\bigoplus_{x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}}{\mathcal{X}}(x\to FI(y))\cong\bigoplus_{v,x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}}{\mathcal{X}}(x\to\overline{v}yv)\cong\bigoplus_{v,x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}}{\mathcal{X}}(vx\to yv)=\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}}).

Moreover, our two commuting
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
-actions correspond to the left and right regular representation.

Now as a
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})-\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
bimodule, the regular representation
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
has one irreducible summand for each type of irreducible representation of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
, i.e. each isomorphism class in
\operatorname{Irr}(Z({\mathcal{X}}))
.
We thus see that the anyon types of the two excitations at the punctures must agree, up to an opposite which occurs due to a left/right action of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
, which translates into an anyon type and its dual at the end of the strings.

Now any local operator is localized away from at least one of the two excitations.
While the local operator can destroy the
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
representation on one side, it is localized away from the other excitation, and therefore commutes with the action of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
at the site of the other excitation.
Hence the local operator still preserves the anyon type at the other puncture.
So if our local operator takes one excitation to another at the same (or nearby) site, then the above argument says it cannot change the anyon type.

We conclude that on a twice-punctured sphere, an irreducible
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
representation type is a complete invariant of a superselection sector.
It is invariant under applying local operators, and any finer invariant would necessarily split irreducible summands of the regular
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
-
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
bimodule, which disrespects the fact that
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
acts by local operators.

2.5
Hopping operators

Hopping operators
[
HGW18
]
translate localized excitations in our system.
The following is an equivalent but more streamlined definition of hopping operator that appears in
[
CGHP23
, 2.2.2]
:

H^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\delta}:=\sum_{y\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})}\sum_{\psi_{y}\in\operatorname{ONB}(X\to y)}B_{p}B_{q}T^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\delta}(\psi_{y},\psi_{y})\pi^{1}_{k},

where
T^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\delta}(\psi,\psi)
is a modified string operator which does not apply
\pi^{1}_{\ell}
at the start, but rather just
\pi^{1}_{\ell,v}
.
Here is a cartoon of the
H^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\delta}
action on an excited state.

We now explain how hopping operators and string operators are compatible.
Given anyons
(X,\sigma_{X}),(Y,\sigma_{Y})\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
, we can first apply the string operator
S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\gamma}(\bullet,\phi)

where
\phi:H\to x
and we suppress the data at the other end of the string,
after which we can apply the hopping operator

H^{(Y,\sigma_{Y})}_{\delta}
.
Here is a cartoon of this setup ignoring the start of
\gamma
:

This immediately implies that

H^{(Y,\sigma_{Y})}_{\delta}S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\gamma}(\bullet,\phi)=\begin{cases}S^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\delta\cdot\gamma}(\bullet,\phi)&\text{if }X=Y\\

where
\delta\cdot\gamma
denotes the concatenation of
\delta
and
\gamma
.

\psi\in\operatorname{ONB}(Y\to x)

3
String net models for enriched unitary fusion categories

In this section we give a rigorous treatment of the enriched Levin-Wen string net model associated to an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
from
[
HBJP23
]
, where
{\mathcal{A}}
is a UMTC representing the Witt class of the anomaly.
In particular, we use TQFT techniques to prove the claim that the boundary excitations are the enriched center/Müger centeralizer
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
of
{\mathcal{A}}
in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
We do so in more generality, starting with an arbitrary unitary braided fusion category
{\mathcal{A}}
and a fully faithful unitary braided functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
.

In the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched model, objects of the form
\Phi(a)\in{\mathcal{X}}
for
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
can be ‘pulled off’ the
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary into the
{\mathcal{A}}
-bulk.
This process shows that the
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
-action induced from string operators on the boundary descends to a quotient of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{S}})
called the
dome algebra
.
We analyze this algebra in §
3.2
and show that it classifies the boundary anyon types in §
3.3
.
We conclude with §
3.4
on point excitations in the bulk and their connection to point excitations on the boundary.

3.1
Enriched skein modules and enriched string nets

Let
{\mathcal{A}}
be a unitary braided fusion category and
{\mathcal{X}}
be a UFC together with a fully faithful braided functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
We denote by
\Phi:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{X}}
the composite
F\circ\Phi^{Z}
where
F:Z({\mathcal{X}})\to{\mathcal{X}}
is the forgetful functor.

Definition 3.1
.

{\mathcal{A}}

{\mathcal{X}}

-boundary points and
n

The diagram on the left hand side above is shorthand, and the black crossings
do not
represent any kind of braiding; rather the diagram is drawn on the surface of a 2-sphere.
As
{\mathcal{X}}
is
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched, we may draw the
{\mathcal{A}}
-string as passing through the 3D bulk inside the 2-sphere.

The total Hilbert space is the tensor product over the local Hilbert spaces.
The Hamiltonian is made of 2 types of terms.
First, for every edge/link
\ell
in our lattice, we have a projector
A_{\ell}
enforcing that labels on edges match.
To define the face/plaquette terms
B_{p}
, we first pass to the image of the projector
P_{A}
onto the ground state of
-\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}A_{\ell}
.
There are three types of
B_{p}
terms:
those in the
{\mathcal{A}}
-bulk, those on plaquettes made of both
{\mathcal{A}}
and
{\mathcal{X}}
-links, and those on the
{\mathcal{X}}
boundary.
We will define the third type rigorously, and leave the first two to the reader.
On these plaquettes, the operator
B_{p}
is given by

(18)

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}\,.

Otherwise,
C(\xi,\eta)=0
.
In particular, the
B_{p}
are self-adjoint, commuting orthogonal projections.

Again, this first inner product picture is meant to be interpreted as the inner product on the enriched skein module
{\mathcal{S}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}4},8)
which can be drawn on a sphere similar to (
17
).

Proof.

K:=\frac{1}{D_{\mathcal{X}}\sqrt{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}d_{a}d_{b}d_{c}d_{d}}d_{s}d_{t}d_{u}d_{v}d_{w}d_{x}d_{y}d_{z}}}.

\{\eta\}
ONB of
{\mathcal{H}}_{v}={\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{X}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathbb{D}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}1},4)
(assuming the internal edges match giving a vector in
P_{A}{\mathcal{H}}_{\operatorname{tot}}
),

{\mathcal{X}}
, we can apply the (

) relation again to ‘unzip’ along the

string to obtain
the claimed formula for
C(\xi,\eta)
.

To see that
B_{p}
is self-adjoint, we simply observe
C(\eta,\xi)=\overline{C(\xi,\eta)}
, and thus the matrix representation of
B_{p}
is self-adjoint with respect to our distinguished ONB
\{\xi\}
for the ground state space of
-\sum_{\ell}A_{\ell}
.
That
B_{p}^{2}=B_{p}
and
[B_{p},B_{q}]=0
for distinct plaquettes
p,q
follows from (
I=H
) and (
Bigon 2
) as depicted in
[
Zha17
, §5.4]
.
∎

Lemma 3.3

(
5=6
)
.

The product of any 5 plaquette operators around a bulk cube is equal to the product of all 6 plaquette operators around the bulk cube, with the exception that the deleted plaquette operator cannot be a boundary
{\mathcal{X}}
-plaquette operator.

The case when the front face is not an
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary plaquette follows from the same manipulation, using that
{\mathcal{A}}
-plaquette operator is an idempotent.
∎

Suppose we have a 3-ball
{\mathcal{B}}
in our lattice, which may intersect the
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary.
We have an
evaluation map

\operatorname{eval}
from the tensor product over the
{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
corresponding to sites
v
in the ball to the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched skein module with the appropriate number of boundary points.
We let
N_{p}(\partial{\mathcal{B}})
denote the number of plaquettes in the interior
of
{\mathcal{B}}
on the
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary,
and we let
N_{p}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})
denote the number of plaquettes in the interior of
{\mathcal{B}}
which are not on the
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary.
(The
B_{p}
terms for
p\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}
sum over simples in
{\mathcal{X}}
, while the
B_{p}
terms for
p\in{\mathcal{B}}^{\circ}
sum over simples in
{\mathcal{A}}
.)
We let
N_{c}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})
denote the number of cubes in the interior of
{\mathcal{B}}
.
The following proposition is the enriched analog of Theorem
2.9
above.

Theorem 3.4
.

Denoting the global dimensions of
{\mathcal{A}},{\mathcal{X}}
by
D_{\mathcal{A}},D_{\mathcal{X}}
respectively,

\prod_{p\subset{\mathcal{B}}}B_{p}=D_{\mathcal{A}}^{-\big(N_{p}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})-N_{c}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})\big)}D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-N_{p}(\partial{\mathcal{B}})}\cdot\operatorname{eval}^{\dagger}\circ\operatorname{eval}.

Proof.

The proof proceeds by adjoining adjacent plaquettes by induction.
We provide the detailed argument for 2 adjacent plaquettes on the
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary, and we leave the remaining details to the reader.
That is, we will prove that the matrix coefficients of
B_{o}B_{p}
for adjacent plaquettes
o,p
are given by

\displaystyle C_{o,p}(\xi^{\prime},\xi)

\xi,\xi^{\prime}
are choices of 6 vectors from our distinguished ONB of
{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
.
Again, we have suppressed shadings on squares for readability.
This will exactly show that for every
\xi,\xi^{\prime}
in an ONB for

{\mathcal{S}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}6},10)
,

\langle\xi|B_{o}B_{p}\xi^{\prime}\rangle_{\bigotimes_{v\in{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}}=D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-2}\langle\operatorname{eval}\xi|\operatorname{eval}\xi^{\prime}\rangle_{{\mathcal{S}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}6},10)}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad B_{o}B_{p}=D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-2}\operatorname{eval}^{\dagger}\circ\operatorname{eval}

on the ball
{\mathcal{B}}
which only contains the 2 boundary plaquettes
o
and
p
.

To ease the notation, we set

\displaystyle K:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}d_{a}\cdots d_{f}}d_{q}\cdots d_{z}}},

\displaystyle K_{o}

\displaystyle:=\frac{\sqrt{d_{j}d_{h}d_{m}d_{g}}}{\sqrt{d_{j^{\prime}}d_{h^{\prime\prime}}d_{m^{\prime}}d_{g^{\prime}}}}

\displaystyle K_{o}^{\prime}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{j}d_{j^{\prime}}d_{h}d_{m}d_{m^{\prime}}d_{g}d_{g^{\prime}}}},

\displaystyle K_{p}(h^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle:=\frac{\sqrt{d_{k}d_{i}d_{\ell}d_{h^{\prime\prime}}}}{\sqrt{d_{k^{\prime}}d_{i^{\prime}}d_{\ell^{\prime}}d_{h^{\prime}}}}

\displaystyle K_{p}^{\prime}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}d_{k^{\prime}}d_{i}d_{i^{\prime}}d_{\ell}d_{\ell^{\prime}}d_{h^{\prime}}}}.

In the calculation below, we label strings and vertices as much as possible, but sometimes we omit labels that can be determined from the previous diagram when the diagram is getting very intricate.
Moreover, since we have fixed
\eta_{i,j}\in\operatorname{ONB}
, some of the sums over simples from the plaquette operators collapse as in the proofs of Lemma
2.8
, Theorem
2.9
, and Proposition
3.2
.
Again, we suppress shaded squares for readability.

This final diagram is exactly the
D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-2}
times the skein module
{\mathcal{S}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}6},10)
inner product.

It remains to account for the exponent of
{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}
for the bulk plaquettes.
To get the correct exponent, we introduce a subset
{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}\subset{\mathcal{B}}^{\circ}
that we obtain by removing exactly one non
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary plaquette from each cube in
{\mathcal{B}}^{\circ}
.
We do so by picking a maximal spanning tree for the dual lattice intersected with
{\mathcal{B}}
, which has a vertex for each cube and an edge for each face between cubes, plus one additional (non
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary) edge connecting our maximal spanning tree to a cube in the bulk outside of
{\mathcal{B}}
.
By Lemma
3.3
, it follows that

\prod\limits_{p\subset{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}}B_{p}=\prod\limits_{p\subset{\mathcal{B}}^{\circ}}B_{p}\,.

The subset
{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}\subset{\mathcal{B}}
is exactly the set of
N_{p}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})-N_{c}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})
plaquettes of
{\mathcal{B}}
which do not intersect this spanning tree.
Just as with the plaquettes on the boundary, we can multiply two plaquette operators which share an edge and compute the matrix coefficients of this new operator.
Since the union of the plaquettes in
{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}
is simply connected, at each inductive step, the resulting enriched skein module is unitarily isomorphic to one of the form
{\mathcal{S}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{D}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m},n)
, via a deformation retraction onto the boundary.
This topological map gives a well defined map on skein modules since
{\mathcal{A}}
is braided; i.e the red strings in the bulk may be unambigously projected onto the boundary via the deformation retraction.
Therefore we may combine all
N_{p}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})-N_{c}({\mathcal{B}}^{\circ})
non
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary plaquettes and compute matrix coefficients analogously to the two plaquette case.
The matrix coefficients have a factor of
D_{\mathcal{A}}^{-1}
for each bulk plaquette in
{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}
.
Further multiplying the bulk plaquettes in
{\mathcal{B}}^{\prime}
with the
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary plaquettes which each contribute a factor of
D_{\mathcal{X}}
,
the result follows.
∎

Remark 3.5
.

We can use enriched skein modules to give another string-net model for a(n uneriched) UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
due to Corey Jones where excitations can be localized on a single vertex rather than an edge and its neighboring plaquettes.
This is similar to Corey Jones’ model presented in
[
CGHP23
]
with extra strands corresponding to a condensable algebra
in order to implement anyon condensation.

Otherwise,
C(\xi,\eta)=0
.
In particular, the
B_{p}
are self-adjoint, commuting orthogonal projections.

Finally, the local Hamiltonian now has
vertex terms

C_{v}
which enforce that the simple label on each blue edge is
1_{Z({\mathcal{X}})}
.
Hence the ground states of

H:=-\sum_{\ell}A_{\ell}-\sum_{p}B_{p}-\sum_{v}C_{v}

are exactly the ground states of the usual string-net model for
{\mathcal{X}}
from §
2.2
.

Now excitations can live on the blue edges, corresponding to a violation of a single
C_{v}
term.
We can detect the type of the excitation as it corresponds to a representation of the abelian
\rm C^{*}
-algebra
{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z({\mathcal{X}}))}
which acts on each blue edge.
Note that this algebra is Morita equivalent to
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
as
\mathsf{Rep}(\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}}))\cong Z({\mathcal{X}})\cong\mathsf{Rep}({\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z({\mathcal{X}}))})
.
These vertex excitations are equivalent to the excitations discussed above in §
2.4
;
indeed, for each
(X,\sigma_{X})\in\operatorname{Irr}(Z({\mathcal{X}}))
and
\psi:F(X)\to x
for
x\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
corresponding to the localized excitation (
13
),
we have the hopping operator

H^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\pi}(\psi):=B_{p}B_{q}T_{\pi}^{(X,\sigma_{X})}(\psi)

as in the cartoon below:

), this extends the excitation all the way to the boundary blue edge.

By (
14
), the hopping operator
H^{(X,\sigma_{X})}_{\pi}(\psi)
takes vectors in the
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
-representation corresponding to
(X,\sigma_{X})\in\operatorname{Irr}(Z({\mathcal{X}}))

to vectors in the
{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z({\mathcal{X}}))}
-representation corresponding to
(X,\sigma_{X})
, establishing the equivalence of the excitations.

3.2
Dome algebra and boundary excitations

In this section, we discuss the analog of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
which will help us classify localized excitations in our enriched model.
For this section,
{\mathcal{X}}
is a unitary fusion category and
{\mathcal{A}}
is a unitary braided tensor subcategory of
Z({\mathcal{X}})
(which need not be modular).
This equips
{\mathcal{X}}
with the structure of an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched fusion category, i.e., a unitary braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
, which in this setting is given by the fully faithful inclusion.
We write
\Phi:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{X}}
for the composite of
\operatorname{Forget}\circ\Phi^{Z}
, where
\operatorname{Forget}:Z({\mathcal{X}})\to{\mathcal{X}}
is the forgetful functor.

The following definition was suggested to us by Corey Jones.

Definition 3.6
.

The
dome algebra

\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})

is the quotient of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
by the

In the final equality above, we used that
Z({\mathcal{X}})
is ribbon.
(Note that unitary tensor functors between UFCs are automatically pivotal.)

The name ‘dome algebra’ comes from thinking about the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
as a unitary module tensor category;

{\mathcal{X}}
corresponds to a 2D boundary of a 3D
{\mathcal{A}}
-bulk.
Pushing a morphism from the
{\mathcal{A}}
-bulk into the boundary corresponds to applying
\Phi=\operatorname{Forget}\circ\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{X}}
.
Morphisms in the image of this action map can be lifted back out into the bulk.
Hence the annuli in the defining relation can be viewed as ‘domes’ (or rather ‘bowls’) where the 2D boundary is an annulus and the
{\mathcal{A}}
-strings lift into the 3D bulk.

Theorem 3.9
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{A}}\subset Z({\mathcal{X}})
is a braided subcategory and
(X,\sigma_{X})\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
The following are equivalent.

1.

(X,\sigma_{X})\in Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
, the Müger centralizer of
{\mathcal{A}}
in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
,

2.

The half-braidings
\sigma_{X,a}
and
\sigma_{a,X}^{-1}

agree in
{\mathcal{X}}(X\Phi(a)\to\Phi(a)X)
,

3.

The half-braidings
\sigma_{X,\Phi(a)}
and
\sigma_{\Phi(a),X}^{-1}
have the same matrix elements, i.e., for every

m\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to y)
,

n\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to z)
,

f\in{\mathcal{X}}(\Phi(a)y\to x)
,
and

g\in{\mathcal{X}}(z\Phi(a)\to x)

for
x,y,z\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
,

4.

The representation of the tube algebra
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
associated to
(X,\sigma_{X})
descends to a representation of the dome algebra
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
.

(3)\Leftrightarrow(4)

3.7
.

Given
(X,\sigma_{X})\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
, the representation
{\mathcal{H}}_{X}
of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
descends to a representation of
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
if and only if for all
m\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to y)
and
n\in{\mathcal{X}}(X\to z)
,

\langle n|\phi\rhd m\rangle_{{\mathcal{X}}(X\to z)}=\langle n|\psi\rhd m\rangle_{{\mathcal{X}}(X\to z)}.

These two expressions are equal for all
m,n
if and only if (3) holds.
∎

3.3
Localized enriched excitations, punctured enriched skein modules, and enriched string operators

We now focus on localized boundary excitations of our
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched
{\mathcal{X}}
-string net model.
Here, localized means that excitations violate (at most) 4 terms in the Hamiltonian, corresponding to a single boundary edge and its 3 adjacent plaquettes.
These excitations can thus be viewed as vectors in a punctured enriched skein module
{\mathcal{S}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}_{\mathcal{X}}({\mathbb{A}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m},n,1)
.
As above, this space carries an action of the
\rm C^{*}
-algebra
{\mathfrak{A}}
from (
9
), which by an isotopy/Morita equivalence argument, can be reduced to an action similar to (
10
) of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
after applying
\pi^{1}_{\ell,v}
.

Proposition 3.10
.

The ideal
{\mathcal{J}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}\subset\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
acts as zero.
Thus the
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
action descends to an action of
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
.

Proof.

We sketch the proof, which is similar to the calculation (
19
).
After applying
\pi^{1}_{\ell,v}
, we have effectively glued two cubes together, resulting in a large rectangular prism with 8
{\mathcal{A}}
-faces and one
{\mathcal{X}}
-face.
The image of our excited state under
\pi^{1}_{\ell,v}
still lies in the images of the 8 plaquette operators which act along the boundary of our rectangular prism.
We now compute

acts as zero.
∎

above,
it is clear from (

) that the dome ideal acts as zero whenever the anyon comes from
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
.

X\in Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})

Z({\mathcal{X}})

Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})^{\operatorname{rev}}
as opposed to
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})\subset Z({\mathcal{X}})
(and suppressing 4th roots),

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}\,.

Remark 3.11
.

As in Remark
2.13
, we can additionally see that isomorphism classes of
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
representations are in bijection with boundary anyon types.
In the case of a twice-punctured sphere with internal
{\mathcal{A}}
-edges,

the space of ground states is now the subspace of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
which is compatible with the
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}
-bulk.
Since
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
is just the quotient of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
obtained by imposing the compatibility relations
{\mathcal{J}}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}
, this is exactly the regular representation of
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
, i.e.
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
as a
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})-\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
bimodule.
An argument similar to Remark
2.13
shows that anyon types are in bijective correspondence with
\operatorname{Irr}(\mathsf{Rep}(\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})))=\operatorname{Irr}(Z^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}}))
.

3.4
Sphere algebra, bulk excitations, and bulk enrichment of boundary

Suppose
{\mathcal{A}}
is an arbitrary UBFC and
{\mathcal{X}}
is an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC such that the unitary braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
is fully faithful.
In this section, we analyze the (3+1)D bulk
{\mathcal{A}}
-excitations and show they are
Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
by constructing representations of the
sphere algebra

\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
, a further quotient of
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{A}})
.
This is consistent with
[
JFR24
, Lem. 2.16]
which states that
\Omega Z(\Sigma{\mathcal{A}})=Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
.
By
[
DNO13
, Prop. 4.3]
,
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
is canonically
Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
-enriched as a UBFC, i.e.,
Z_{2}(Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}))=Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
.
We realize this enrichment by using hopping operators to bring bulk excitations into the boundary.

The following definition was suggested to us by Corey Jones.

We see that if
\phi:ca\to ac
and
\psi:da\to ad
, then
\phi\psi-\psi\phi\in{\mathcal{J}}
:

\displaystyle\phi\psi-\psi\phi

\displaystyle=\phi\psi-\lambda(\phi)\psi+\lambda(\phi)\psi-\lambda(\phi)\lambda(\psi)+\underbrace{\lambda(\phi)\lambda(\psi)}_{=\lambda(\psi)\lambda(\phi)}-\lambda(\psi)\phi+\lambda(\psi)\phi-\psi\phi

\displaystyle=\big(\phi-\lambda(\phi)\big)\psi+\lambda(\phi)\big(\psi-\lambda(\psi)\big)+\lambda(\psi)\big(\lambda(\phi)-\phi\big)+\big(\lambda(\psi)-\psi\big)\phi\in{\mathcal{J}}.

The next lemma gives an abstract characterization of
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
.

Lemma 3.13
.

The following
*
-algebras are isomorphic:

1.

\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
,

2.

T_{2}/(T_{2}\cap{\mathcal{J}})
where
T_{2}\subset\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
is the subalgebra spanned by
\phi:ca\to bc
for
a,b,c\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{A}})
such that
a=b\in Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
, and

3.

{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))}
.

Proof.

First, given

a,b,c\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{A}})

and

\phi:ca\to bc
in
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{A}})
,
if
a\neq b
, then
\phi\in{\mathcal{J}}
.
If
a\neq b
, then
\lambda(\phi)=0
, so

\phi=\phi-\lambda(\phi)\in{\mathcal{J}}
.

Second, suppose
a\notin\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))
, and pick
c\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{A}})
whose
S
-matrix entry
S_{a,c}\neq d_{a}d_{c}
.
We claim that
\operatorname{id}_{a}\in{\mathcal{J}}
.
Indeed,

By the second isomorphism theorem,
T_{2}/(T_{2}\cap{\mathcal{J}})\cong(T_{2}+{\mathcal{J}})/{\mathcal{J}}
.
By the two facts proven above, every representative of an element of
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
in
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{A}})
can be taken from
T_{2}
.
This means the
*
-algebra map
(T_{2}+{\mathcal{J}})/{\mathcal{J}}\to\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})

given by

x+{\mathcal{J}}\mapsto x+{\mathcal{J}}

is onto and thus an isomorphism.

By the two facts proven above, the map
\delta_{a}\mapsto\operatorname{id}_{a}+T_{2}\cap{\mathcal{J}}
is a surjective
*
-algebra map
{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))}\to T_{2}/(T_{2}\cap{\mathcal{J}})
.
The inverse is given by
\lambda|_{T_{2}}
, which descends to
T_{2}/(T_{2}\cap{\mathcal{J}})
since
T_{2}\cap{\mathcal{J}}\subset\ker(\lambda|_{T_{2}})
.
∎

The proof of the following theorem is similar to Theorem
3.9
and omitted.
The equivalences of (1)-(4) below are all well known; e.g., see
[
Müg03
, Lem. 7.5]
.

Theorem 3.14
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{A}}
is a braided fusion category.
The following are equivalent.

1.

a\in Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
, the Müger center of
{\mathcal{A}}
,

2.

The braidings
\beta_{a,b}
and
\beta_{b,a}^{-1}

agree for all
b\in{\mathcal{A}}
,

3.

The two canonical lifts of
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
to the Drinfeld center
Z({\mathcal{A}})
agree,

4.

The braidings
\beta_{a,b}
and
\beta_{b,a}^{-1}
have the same matrix elements, i.e.,
for every

m\in{\mathcal{A}}(a\to c)
,

,

,

5.

The representation of the tube algebra
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{A}})
associated to
(a,\beta_{a})
descends to a representation of the sphere algebra
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
.

Remark 3.15
.

While the sphere algebra is similar to the dome algebra, representations of the former correspond to
Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
, while representations of the latter gives
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{A}})
, the centralizer
Z({\mathcal{A}})
of
A
in
Z({\mathcal{A}})
.
The canonical quotient map
\operatorname{Dome}^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{A}})\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
corresponds to the inclusion
Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})\hookrightarrow Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{A}})
.

Similar to (
10
) above, we have a
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{A}})
-action on any state with a localized bulk excitation.
Here, localized means that the bulk Hamiltonian is violated at (at most) 5 terms, namely one edge term and the 4 neighboring plaquette terms.
By a Morita equivalence argument similar to that in §
2.4
, it again suffices to consider the
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{A}})
-action at a single edge
\ell
connected to one vertex of the form

Fact 3.16

(
[
DNO13
, Prop. 4.3]
)
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{X}}
is an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC, where the braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
is full.
The Müger center of the enriched center
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
is
Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
.

Remark 3.17
.

The above lemma clearly fails when the braided functor
{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
is not full.
For example, consider
{\mathcal{A}}=\mathsf{Rep}(G)
and
{\mathcal{X}}=\mathsf{Vect}
and
{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})=\mathsf{Vect}
is the forgetful functor.

Given a bulk excitation
a\in\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))
,
for every

\psi:\Phi(a)\to x
where
x\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
,
we can define the
bulk-to-boundary hopping operator

H^{(a,\beta_{a})}_{\pi}(\psi):=B_{o}B_{p}B_{q}B_{r}T_{\pi}^{(a,\beta_{a})}(\psi)\pi_{k}^{1}

as in the cartoon below.

\scriptstyle a
\scriptstyle\psi

That is, since
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))}
, the
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
-representation at our bulk edge
\ell
and vertex
v
must be labelled by the simple object
a
.
We apply
\pi^{1}_{k}
at the boundary edge
k
, we extend
a
along the path
\pi

placing
\psi
at the end to get a simple
x\in\operatorname{Irr}({\mathcal{X}})
on the boundary,
and finally we apply the 4 bulk plaquette operators
B_{o}B_{p}B_{q}B_{r}
which meet the bulk edge
\ell
.

By (
14
), the bulk-to-boundary hopping operator
H^{(a,\beta_{a})}_{\pi}(\psi)
takes vectors in the
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
-representation corresponding to
a\in\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))

to vectors in the
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
-representation corresponding to
\Phi^{Z}(a)
.
Thus the hopping operator physically demonstrates that
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
is a
Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
-enriched UBFC
[
DNO13
, Prop. 4.3]
.

The above discussion is sub-optimal, as the hopping operator depends on a choice of
\psi
.
This problem occurs because we have pushed
a\in{\mathcal{A}}
into
{\mathcal{X}}
via
\Phi
, and
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
is not actually a quotient of
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
, but only Morita equivalent to a quotient.
If we instead use a model for the boundary where boundary excitations can be hosted at a single vertex as in Remark
3.5
above,

we can avoid the choice of
\psi
altogether.
Indeed,
{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))}
is an honest quotient of
{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}}))}
, which is the algebra of local operators (Morita equivalent to
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{\mathcal{A}}}}({\mathcal{X}})
) acting at this type of ancilla.
In this setting, we can define the bulk-to-boundary hopping operator by

H_{\pi}^{(a,\beta_{a})}:=B_{o}B_{p}B_{q}B_{r}T_{\pi}^{(a,\beta_{a})}

as in the cartoon below:

\scriptstyle a

Now using the isomorphism
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))}
from Remark
3.13
, we see that this hopping operator intertwines the
\operatorname{Sphere}({\mathcal{A}})
-action coming from the bulk with the
{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}}))}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{\operatorname{Irr}(Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}}))}
-action hosted on the blue edges.

4
Conclusion

In this manuscript, we have reviewed the explicit construction of the 2D boundary boundary theory of the 3D Walker-Wang model given from
[
HBJP23
]
by a UMTC
\mathcal{A}
as a sort of enriched Levin-Wen model based on an
\mathcal{A}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
.
Using techniques from TQFT, we have confirmed the prediction of
[
HBJP23
]
that the excitations of this 2D model are given by the enriched center/Müger centralizer
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
of
\mathcal{A}
in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
We achieved this by defining the algebra
\operatorname{Dome}^{{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{X}})
and showing that its irreducible representations are in one-to-one correspondence with the excitations of the boundary theory.
This is analogous to how the irreducible representations of the tube algebra
\operatorname{Tube}({\mathcal{X}})
are in one-to-one correspondence of the excitations of an unenriched Levin-Wen model given by a UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
.

All of these arguments are made on finite lattices.
There is also an operator algebraic approach
[
Naa17
]
for identifying excitation types on infinite lattices.
It would be interesting to check that the excitation types on the infinite lattice align with those from our analysis.

In our construction, we have not considered protection by 0-form symmetries.
A direction for future research would be to endow the bulk theory with such a symmetry and to study the excitations in the resulting anomalous
G
-enriched topological order in the 2D boundary theory.
